narrative:
The model determined that you have a 76% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the law school decided to reject your application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your class rank in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your family income bracket. Your third-year class rank was by far the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (compared with an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) signaled that your academic performance in the later stages of law school was substantially weaker than what the model sees in students who ultimately pass the bar.

Your LSAT score of 25 was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. It sits well below the average of 37 among students who were admitted. In contrast, your family income being in the lower-middle bracket actually worked slightly in your favor; students from that background are relatively uncommon in the admitted group, yet the model saw this as a modest positive signal rather than a negative one.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of low class standing and low LSAT created too high a risk of bar exam failure to justify admission.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance and retaking the LSAT. Raising both your class rank and test score would directly address the two biggest reasons for this rejection and substantially improve your chances in a future application.
